clinicalPearls: Selective vulnerability to weakly virulent mycobacteria (the BCG vaccine strain and environmental non-tuberculous mycobacteria) and to non-typhoidal Salmonella in a child who otherwise appears immunologically well.
An umbrella term for genetically heterogeneous defects along the IL-12/IL-23-interferon-gamma circuit that couples mononuclear phagocytes with T and natural killer cells.
Disseminated BCG disease following neonatal vaccination is a classic sentinel presentation.
The specific genotype matters: complete interferon-gamma receptor defects behave very differently from IL-12/IL-23 axis defects in severity and treatment response.
Recombinant interferon-gamma helps in IL-12/IL-23 axis and partial receptor defects but is futile in complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency or STAT1 loss-of-function.
Granuloma quality is informative: poorly formed, multibacillary, lepromatous-like lesions suggest severe interferon-gamma signalling failure.
Consider the diagnosis in any child with recurrent or disseminated environmental mycobacterial or salmonella infection, even without a family history.
Live BCG and other live vaccines are contraindicated once the diagnosis is suspected.
reference.pathophysiology: MSMD arises from inborn errors that disrupt the interleukin-12/interleukin-23-dependent production of interferon-gamma and the interferon-gamma-mediated activation of mononuclear phagocytes. Myeloid cells secrete IL-12 and IL-23, which act through receptors sharing the IL-12 receptor beta-1 chain on T and natural killer cells to drive interferon-gamma release; interferon-gamma then signals through the IFNGR1/IFNGR2 receptor and STAT1 to license macrophages to kill intracellular organisms. Autosomal recessive or dominant defects in IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, IL12RB2, IL23R, STAT1, IRF8, ISG15, TYK2, JAK1, RORC, TBX21, SPPL2A and the macrophage-specific respiratory-burst component CYBB each interrupt this circuit at a different point, producing a shared phenotype of impaired containment of poorly virulent mycobacteria and Salmonella. The amount of residual pathway function determines whether disease is mild and localised or severe and disseminated.
additionalDifferentials: Severe combined and other combined immunodeficiencies
HIV infection and other causes of acquired CD4 lymphopenia
Anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome (an acquired adult phenocopy)
GATA2 deficiency with disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease
Disseminated tuberculosis in an apparently immunocompetent host
NEMO/IKK-gamma deficiency and other syndromic immunodeficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Whole-exome or targeted inborn-errors-of-immunity gene panel sequencing
Flow cytometry for interferon-gamma receptor and IL-12 receptor beta-1 surface expression
Functional whole-blood assays of interferon-gamma production after BCG/IL-12 stimulation and of STAT1 phosphorylation
Plasma interferon-gamma and IL-12 concentrations, whose pattern helps localise the defect
Mycobacterial culture with species identification and molecular typing to distinguish BCG from environmental strains
Screening for anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies in older patients to exclude the acquired phenocopy
Histology of affected tissue for granuloma morphology and bacillary load
redFlags: Disseminated or persistent infection following live BCG vaccination
Recurrent non-tuberculous mycobacterial or invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease in a child
Poorly formed, multibacillary granulomata on biopsy
Failure of appropriately treated mycobacterial infection to respond to standard antimicrobials
Family history of childhood death from disseminated mycobacterial or salmonella infection
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the specific genetic lesion and residual pathway function: IL-12/IL-23 axis and partial receptor defects often do well with prolonged antimicrobials and adjunctive interferon-gamma, whereas complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency carries high mortality and may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal basic immune screen (immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets, neutrophil oxidative burst) excludes the diagnosis, since these are typically normal.
Giving recombinant interferon-gamma to a child with complete receptor deficiency, in whom it cannot work.
Labelling BCG-derived disease as tuberculosis without species typing.
Dismissing the diagnosis because there is no family history, as many cases are sporadic or arise from consanguineous but unaffected parents.
Administering further live vaccines before immunological evaluation.
references: International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS) inborn errors of immunity classification
management: Prolonged combination antimycobacterial therapy directed by species identification and susceptibility testing, with duration extended in poorly controlled disease

Adjunctive recombinant interferon-gamma for interleukin-12/interleukin-23-axis and partial receptor defects, avoided as ineffective in complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency and STAT1 loss-of-function
Avoidance of live vaccines including BCG, with active treatment of disseminated BCG disease
Antimicrobial cover for non-typhoidal Salmonella and antifungal therapy for susceptible intramacrophage fungi when they arise
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency, where mortality is otherwise high
Regular monitoring for relapse, new intracellular infection and cumulative drug toxicity
Genetic counselling and cascade testing of relatives given the Mendelian inheritance
Multidisciplinary care through clinical immunology and infectious disease services
